articles.title_orig: Israeli Spy Chief Pressed for Renewed Iran Strikes During U.S. Visit
articles.title_zh: Israeli Spy Chief Pressed for Renewed Iran Strikes During U.S. Visit
articles.content_orig:
Container ships are seen through haze in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. (Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA via AP)
CAIRO (AP) — Iran widened its attacks on its Gulf neighbors on Wednesday, targeting a U.S. air base in Kuwait and launching several attacks on Bahrain in what appeared to be retaliation for American strikes the day before.
After about two months without such attacks, Iran has repeatedly targeted U.S. facilities in Bahrain in recent days. The small Persian Gulf island kingdom hosts the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet.
The early morning attacks in the nearly nine-month-old war came after a U.S. fighter jet struck a Revolutionary Guard missile launch site Tuesday on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz . The U.S. strike was in retaliation for an Iranian attack on an American radar installation in Bahrain earlier Tuesday.
Iran said that its recent attacks — including those on other U.S. facilities in Bahrain on Sunday and Friday — were in response to U.S. drone surveillance operations and an attack on Iranian communications towers.
AP correspondent Charles de Ledesma reports Iran has fired on a U.S. air base in Kuwait and at targets in Bahrain.
The tit-for-tat attacks come as the commander of the U.S. military’s Central Command, Adm. Brad Cooper, met Wednesday in Tel Aviv with Israel’s military chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, and the director of Israel’s intelligence agency Mossad, Roman Gofman.
They also complicate negotiations for a diplomatic solution and raise the risk of resumption of all-out conflict as a conflict in Yemen between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and a Saudi-led coalition could drag on for months.
The U.S. military didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the latest attacks.
With its economy suffering under a U.S. naval blockade and American military escorts helping restore the passage of oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, experts say that the recent attacks suggest Tehran may be growing weary of the status quo.
“Even if neither side intends to enter a broader confrontation, the accumulation of military incidents across multiple fronts increases the risk of miscalculation and escalation beyond what either side originally intended,” Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X following the initial reports of the attack on Kuwait.
U.S. President Donald Trump has sent mixed messages on his next steps, saying new strikes are highly unlikely , but also sending a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East.
Though U.S. military protection has helped restore oil shipments from the Gulf, Iran has continued to attack tankers as they attempt to transit the Strait of Hormuz.
United Arab Emirates state-owned oil company ADNOC said Wednesday that one of its tanker crew members was missing after an attack in the strait on Tuesday, while 11 others were injured and were receiving medical care.
Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies and a former Iran specialist in Israel’s military and intelligence services, described an “increasingly clear” pattern of attacks by Iran on shipping and U.S. facilities in the Gulf region.
“Iran appears to be pursuing a strategy of deliberate, calibrated escalation,” he wrote in an analysis on X. “The objective is not necessarily to trigger an all-out war, but to steadily increase the military, economic, and political costs of maintaining the blockade.”
He said that Washington is faced with the dilemma that a limited response may encourage Iran to push further, while a stronger response risks accelerating the escalation that the U.S. is trying to avoid.
“As long as the U.S. naval blockade remains in place and no agreement is reached, further escalation will become increasingly difficult to avoid,” he said. “There are two clear paths to de-escalation: a negotiated agreement or a U.S. decision to lift the blockade.”
After Israel and the U.S. attacked Iran on Feb. 28 to launch the war, Iran regularly fired on American facilities and interests in neighboring Gulf countries, as well as energy infrastructure and other targets.
In the attack early Wednesday on the Ali Al Salem air base in Kuwait, the Iranian military fired at air defense systems and drone and missile launch platforms, according to a report on Iran’s state broadcaster.
Kuwait’s military said that its air defenses had intercepted drone attacks and didn’t immediately report any damage. The Kuwaiti Foreign Ministry condemned the repeated Iranian attacks as “criminal,” saying that they threatened the country’s security and stability.
During the war, Ali Al Salem Air Base has been struck at least 30 times by Iran, damaging or destroying at least 15 aircraft hangars, numerous warehouses and 10 buildings near a residential area, according to an analysis by The Associated Press .
The AP’s analysis used satellite imagery from multiple providers to help determine that Iran’s strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases in the Middle East focused on early-warning systems before hitting aircraft and buildings, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage .
AP also spoke to four regional officials who were briefed or had firsthand knowledge of what was hit. The AP found that, through August, more than 115 drone or missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with U.S. equipment.
Under questioning before a U.S. Senate committee Tuesday about damage to the Navy’s regional headquarters in Bahrain, Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said he couldn’t offer a full damage assessment in Bahrain because “it’s a nonpermissive area for us to go.” He told a reporter months ago that Iran “blew the hell out of Bahrain.”
Meanwhile, Bahrain’s Interior Ministry issued two alerts early Wednesday urging people to take shelter, followed by the “all clear” a short time later. The country’s military later said that it had intercepted a number of attacks from Iran, but gave no information on any damage or casualties.
Saudi officials have briefed allies that the conflict with the Houthis could last for another six months, according to a diplomat familiar with the matter.
The diplomat, who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity, added that the kingdom in diplomatic talks is making the case that the military alliance working to restore the internationally recognized government in Yemen still must further set back the Houthis before it can begin credible talks with the rebel group.
The Iranian-backed Houthis control a significant swath of Yemen, including the capital of Sanaa, and have made territorial gains along the Red Sea coast in the current conflagration. They’ve also rattled the kingdom with missile and drone attacks targeting Saudi infrastructure, including on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and energy infrastructure.
The kingdom continues to make the case to allies that U.S. military support could help change the course of the war in the Saudi-led coalition’s favor, the diplomat said. But thus far, Trump has resisted the push from his ally for U.S. strikes on the Houthis.
Rising reported from Bangkok and Madhani reported from Washington.

articles.title_orig: Iranians are escalating attacks on Strait of Hormuz because they believe they can force Trump into a deal: experts
articles.title_zh: Iranians are escalating attacks on Strait of Hormuz because they believe they can force Trump into a deal: experts
articles.content_orig:
Iran is escalating its attacks in the Middle East as a means to reclaim its control over the Strait of Hormuz and force the US into action for a conclusive end to the war, according to multiple reports.
With about 8 million barrels of oil still exiting through the strait every day under a US naval escort, I ran has stepped up its attacks on tankers to try and stop the flow.
At least six strikes have been confirmed by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations in the past week, with Iran claiming even more attacks at a pace not seen since the war first began.
Tehran has repeatedly stated that it would not allow ships to undermine its claim to the oil chokehold, with Iran specifically targeting the busiest ships that have been making the dangerous back-and-forth trips, according to the Vortexa maritime firm.
The Islamic Republic has also targeted US bases in Bahrain and Kuwait in recent days, a clear escalation meant to challenge the current status quo.
While Trump has signaled that he is content with allowing the war to remain cold as America’s economic pressure campaign squeezes Iran, the Islamic Republic does not have the luxury to wait around.
“The two sides have very different calculations about the costs of prolonging the confrontation,” Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera .
“As economic pressure mounts, Iran may become increasingly willing to take military risks to break the deadlock.”
Lead Iranian negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf signaled this very stance during his address to parliament on Sunday, warning the US that lawmakers were told by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to end the current stalemate.
“We will not remain in a state of ‘neither war nor peace,’” Ghalibaf said. “It makes absolutely no difference to us whether the United States wants negotiations or war.”
The attacks also serve as a way for Iran to show the US and its allies that Tehran has rebuilt its missile and drone launchers and is prepared for all-out war to resume, Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, a Middle East expert at Rice University’s Baker Institute, told the Wall Street Journal.
“The attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain are a signal that Iran retains both the capability and the intent to target US partners across the Gulf and are a reminder to leaders in the Gulf states that they remain vulnerable to retaliation for U.S. actions in the Strait of Hormuz,” Coates Ulrichsen said.
“As the Trump administration continues its buildup of force in the region, the attacks are a reminder that the US does not have a monopoly on the escalation ladder,” he added.

By DAVID WILCOCK, DEPUTY POLITICAL EDITOR and JASON GROVES, POLITICAL EDITOR
Published: 06:09 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 08:59 EST, 19 November 2026
Andy Burnham will join European leaders in a show of solidarity with Ukraine today, hours after Donald Trump took part in an astonishing summit with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping .
The Prime Minister is chairing a meeting of 'Coalition of the Willing' countries in Berlin after announcing Britain will supply a further 1,000 long-range strike drones to Kyiv and jointly fund two £100 million attack boats with Norway.
But the meeting will have to deal with the fallout from the meeting between the leaders of the US, Russia and China in Shenzhen.
Ministers were already nervous that the US President could agree a stitch-up that weakens Ukraine as the war with Russia enters another winter.
He greeted Putin by describing him as a 'friend' with whom he was 'really making history', adding: 'No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.'
Putin, fresh from a setback in his war against Ukraine after the crippling of a key bridge linking Crimea to Russia, said the three countries have 'numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine'.
The Prime Minister, pictured with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, will co-chair a meeting of 'Coalition of the Willing' countries in Berlin
But the meeting will have to deal with the fallout from the meeting between the leaders of the US, Russia and China in Shenzhen
Speaking in the Commons yesterday, Mr Burnham declined to comment on the Shenzhen summit directly, but said: 'When that meeting is taking place in China I will be in Berlin for a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing.
'The thing that we need to do is continue to stand squarely by Ukraine, and that is what this Government will do.'
He said that Britain was united in its support for Ukraine, adding: 'On this issue, let that clear message go out as that meeting takes place in China: this country is squarely with Ukraine.
'We know who the aggressor is in this situation, and we will not in any way deflect from continuing that support.'
The PM last night unveiled a £260million package of direct support for Ukraine.
The package includes 1,000 long-range drones capable of delivering heavy warheads to strike military targets at distances of more than 600 miles.
Putin, fresh from a setback in his war against Ukraine after the crippling of a key bridge linking Crimea to Russia, said the three countries have 'numerous shared interests'
The UK will also build and deliver maritime, logistical and surveillance drones to assist Ukraine in resupplying frontline forces with vital supplies like blood and fridges to hold medicines.
It follows agreement in recent days for Britain to bolster Ukraine's air defences and impose tighter sanctions on Russian oil producers.
The move comes as Putin targets civilian infrastructure in a bid to break Ukrainian morale during the cruel winter months when temperatures regularly drop to minus 20 degrees.
In recent weeks, Ukraine has faced more than 2,000 Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure, leaving civilians without heat or power.
In parts of the country, including the capital Kyiv, energy and water blackouts are now a daily occurrence, sometimes lasting up to 22 hours at a time as engineers battle to restore supplies.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: 'Putin uses winter as a weapon in Ukraine. We are converting our steadfast commitment for Ukraine into capability that will help defend against Russia's barbaric attacks on civilians.
'Ukraine's frontline is the frontline for freedom and democracy, and we will stand with them for as long as it takes.'

TPG is nearing an agreement to acquire US payments automation company Bill Holdings and take it private, the Financial Times has reported.
The proposed transaction could be agreed in the coming days and would place a premium on Bill's current $4.8bn market value, according to sources.
Those people said negotiations remain subject to change.
The timetable could move, or the talks may not result in an agreement.
Elliott Management and Starboard Value became top-10 shareholders in Bill last year.
Both activist investors called on the company to explore a sale after its market capitalisation declined by more than 80% from its 2021 peak of $34bn.
Bill later agreed a truce with Starboard and appointed four new directors to its board.
The company automates payments for small to medium-sized companies and handles more than $300bn in transactions each year.
The FT reported last year that Bill was seeking to win larger customers, which offer more consistent cash flows, and raise the fees earned on each transaction.
TPG has previously invested in the payments sector.
Last year, it agreed a $2.2bn acquisition of Bill rival AvidXchange, along with Corpay.
The reported approach comes as private equity firms assess listed payments and financial technology companies whose shares have performed below broader markets.
Earlier this year, Advent International and Stripe proposed acquiring digital payments company PayPal. That proposal has not produced a deal.
CD&R and GTCR have paused their reported interest in payments processor Global Payments.
Reuters, citing sources, said the firms considered an acquisition in recent weeks but did not progress beyond early discussions because of the challenge of financing a take-private deal of that size.
The firms could return to talks with Global Payments at a later stage.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?
articles.title_zh: Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic's historic IPO — the largest in U.S. history — delivered a big win for the company and its investors. But it failed at another task: reviving animal spirits in the AI trade.
The Nasdaq Composite closed down 2.25% amid a broader market pullback with the S&P 500 declining 2% to 7,175.
It wasn't supposed to play out this way.
Investors had been looking forward to the Anthropic IPO as a "clearing event" — reviving the tech sector after months of choppy trading, the Nvidia espionage scandal, and growing concerns that AI chip sales to Asia are likely to slump as Washington cracks down on potential violations of export controls.
Some of those worries resurfaced Thursday as a short seller, Hunterbrook Media, alleged in a report that firmware sold by chipmaker AMD had turned up in U.S.-blacklisted companies. AMD stock closed down more than 7%. The chipmaker told CNBC it complies with U.S. law.
Adding to the worries, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents showing that a subagency of the Commerce Department approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies. That also raised the prospect of an Asia sales slowdown under stricter export controls.
Many investors and analysts continue to express confidence in the AI trade, noting that Anthropic's successful market debut — the stock closed up 17% from its IPO price and raised more than $81 billion — bodes well for capital spending across tech.
But investors acknowledged that this is a high-tension moment and said it's time to be more strategic about the trade.
Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, described himself as a "circumspect bull," making the comparison to market conditions in 2022 when the big indices tanked in the back half of the year.
"You could have still made money that year. You just needed to have the right combination of longs and shorts," he said.
Part of the challenge, Niles said, has been a price war between the two cutting-edge frontier labs, Anthropic and OpenAI. That has posed a threat to the overall revenue and profit potential of AI and the capex going into it. Fierce competition on price is producing collective losses between the two top companies, he notes.
"The combined revenue growth for OpenAI plus Anthropic went from growing 75% sequentially in Q2 to 48% in Q3," he told CNBC. "The combined losses went from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion from Q2 to Q3."
While uncertainty is high now, some resolution may be on the horizon if a greater degree of commercial and regulatory clarity emerges over the next few months.
Trading experts also told CNBC that the tech sector's troubles Thursday were a more serious matter than Anthropic simply siphoning capital from other parts of the market.
"There's a reset of AI in general," said JJ Kinahan, senior vice president at Cboe Global Markets .
Investors for years have profited in tech by buying the dip, he said, but "there's been an attitude change that [you] can't buy things blindly and they'll all go up." Nvidia's ongoing declines have shaken confidence in the buy-the-dip strategy, he said.
Anthropic's next few trading days will be a key gauge of the market's strength. Friday will be a "wild card," Kinahan said. It could be a "final flush out" for the market, or a bounce that leaves the market in "no man's land" while volatility remains elevated.
A better gauge may be Monday, when options on Anthropic start trading, providing insight into whether retail investors will back the company in force — providing more of a vote of confidence in the AI trade.
"If people think we're going up [on Anthropic] they'll buy stock, but retail particularly will just buy calls," he said. "There's a bigger test coming Monday."
For now, investors continue to sell AI-related stocks.
Neoclouds, the generally highly indebted AI-dedicated computing providers at the outer edges of the AI trade, were down substantially Thursday, with CoreWeave closing down more than 6%.
Hyperscalers such as Alphabet and Amazon.com , viewed as relatively defensive AI bets, also finished lower.
One bright spot: Cybersecurity stocks continued to rally, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike both closing up. AI is finding security holes across software infrastructure, creating a scramble to patch the vulnerabilities before hackers can exploit them.
— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi, Putin sit down for a rare meeting in China
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi, Putin sit down for a rare meeting in China
articles.content_orig:
President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin sat down together in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday in a rare face-to-face encounter for the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries, but there appeared to be little concrete to show for the meeting in terms of resolving any of the crises facing the world.
The leaders offered a joint statement after their roughly hour-and-a-half-long meeting. Mr. Trump immediately left for his return flight to the U.S. without speaking to journalists on the ground. On the flight home, the president said on social media he will hold a press conference at noon on Friday to discuss the trip.
The presidents discussed Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine , which Mr. Trump has wanted to bring to a negotiated end. But the only significant statement on the conflict came after the meeting from Putin, who ruled out any direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing a major strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces on a key bridge in Russian-held Crimea.
Putin's senior aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the meeting that the atmosphere had been good, and the Kremlin quickly released what it called a joint statement from all three leaders characterizing the talks. The White House later provided the same statement.
The three men "exchanged views in detail on the current international situation and reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security," the readout said, adding that as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, they had "reaffirmed their commitment to reforming the UN so that it can more effectively respond to global challenges and fulfill its fundamental mission in the area of international peace and security."
They also committed to increasing gas and oil production "for the benefit of all countries," agreed on the "fundamental importance" of "the principle of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials," and said the " International Criminal Court and other similar bodies should not abuse their powers."
Finally, the leaders "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war, and that it should never be unleashed."
The White House indicated that Mr. Trump might speak with reporters on Air Force One during the flight back to the U.S.
The Kremlin shared a short video on social media, via Russian state media, showing Xi accompanying Putin as they walked out of the meeting to Putin's waiting motorcade. Before they exit the building, Putin is seen shaking Xi's hand, thanking him for hosting the gathering and telling him, according to Russian state media, that nobody had expected it to go so well.
Before the meeting, Mr. Trump met separately with Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and then with Xi.
"We've had a great relationship for many years," Mr. Trump said, standing alongside his Russian counterpart. "I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start."
As Mr. Trump approached Putin for a handshake, he said, "Who is that?" before laughing and saying, "He's my friend."
Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine, who sits on the Committee on Foreign Relations, said the image of Mr. Trump standing with Xi and Putin was concerning.
"Some of the pictures troubled me, seeing the president stand with Putin and Xi, rather than seeing the president stand with the leaders of the global democracies," Kaine said. "When I saw them, it turned my stomach a bit, and particularly President Trump's declaration that Vladimir Putin was a friend. Vladimir Putin is not a friend, and so you know he was either being insincere or he is deeply deluded if he thinks Vladimir Putin is a friend."
In a phone call with NBC reporter Gabe Gutierrez, Mr. Trump called the meeting a 12 on a scale of zero to 10.
Russia's TASS news agency said the war in Ukraine was the main topic discussed by the two leaders, and that Putin left the meeting in "an excellent mood."
After the trilateral talks Thursday, Putin told reporters that Ukraine and Europe were "not yet ready" to make the compromises necessary to resolve the war, according to Russian media.
"We will not negotiate after the attacks on the Crimean bridge," he declared, referring to this week's Ukrainian strike on the highly symbolic Kerch Bridge, which links Russia with Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Putin said Kyiv and Europe would eventually come to understand that it is better to make compromises than to face "realities."
Ukraine and its European partners have long feared that the White House appears willing to offer Putin too much — including the prospect of major energy deals — with no significant concessions from Russia  in return, while putting pressure on Kyiv to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.
Mr. Trump then met for about an hour with Xi ahead of the three-way meeting. As the Trump-Xi session began, Xi told Mr. Trump relations between China and the United States were "stable and improved."
Mr. Trump told reporters he had spoken with Xi for two hours on Wednesday, with trade and tariffs being the main topics. He also said he would be asking China to "do some more" for American farmers, because China has an "insatiable appetite."
Mr. Trump said previously that he planned to talk about denuclearization with his fellow leaders. Russia and the United States are by far the world's largest holders of nuclear weapons , with stockpiles estimated at well over 5,000 warheads, while China is believed to be a distant third, with about 600 weapons.
Putin has made denuclearization a key talking point for decades, but both he and Mr. Trump have allowed previous treaties intended to limit nuclear proliferation to lapse in recent years. China, which has been building up its nuclear program , ruled out taking part in any denuclearization talks with the U.S. and Russia as recently as last year .
China's state-run Xinhua news agency quoted Xi , however, as saying ahead of the trilateral meeting on Thursday that nuclear weapons were a "sword of Damocles hanging over humanity," and calling for them to be "completely banned and completely destroyed, leading to a world free of nuclear weapons."
The Kremlin said in its readout of the three-way meeting that it would "continue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons" with China and the U.S.
A range of other global challenges lingered in the background of the trilateral meeting, including the war in Iran and tension over trade and artificial intelligence .
The summit took place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang , whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed , is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing.
Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire.
Mr. Trump brought up AI during a speech at the APEC forum earlier in the day, vowing to block any "globalist regulation" of artificial int

articles.title_orig: Amazon fights the Delivery Protection Act with homepage banner, in-app pop-up
articles.title_zh: Amazon fights the Delivery Protection Act with homepage banner, in-app pop-up
articles.content_orig:
In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill.
When I log into Amazon today, I’m met with a vertical banner that reads: “ATTENTION NYC Council could add up to $5 per order” with a button that says “Act now.”
I also saw a smaller version of the notice on an order confirmation page on Amazon’s website. The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn’t specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I’m logged into Amazon.
Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518 ), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses.
Clicking on “Act now” on Amazon’s homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states:
Right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.
It’s not unusual for Amazon to take a stance on political matters, and it has publicly opposed the Delivery Protection Act since April . What is new is Amazon using its online marketplace to push a political view. It’s uncommon to see a pop-up about legislation when visiting a shopping website.
The messaging suggests that Amazon is concerned about the potential impact the proposed law would have on its costs. Besides Amazon, the bill targets any company with last-mile delivery facilities in NYC, like FedEx and DoorDash.
It also raises questions about the potential impact on shoppers should Amazon expand its use of its e-commerce platform for additional political messaging. The pop-up launched today impacts only NYC residents but sets a precedent for Amazon to sway political views on other issues. Amazon has made similar moves internally, including reportedly using an app for its employees to campaign against unionizing. But the new pop-up shows Amazon extending that strategy directly to its users.
Given Amazon’s considerable influence in commerce, other companies could copy its actions. Uber and Lyft have previously done so, CNBC reports .
Finally, there’s the question of whether Amazon is fairly depicting the situations surrounding the bill. Notable supporters of the Delivery Protection Act include NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Amazon division of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. Using a platform with massive reach to communicate only one side of an ongoing debate could lead to misinformation and a skewed public perception.
The Delivery Protection Act is currently stalled in the City Council’s Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection. The last hearing on the bill was in April. A committee vote on whether to advance the act to the full City Council hasn’t been set.

articles.title_orig: Leaders of China, Russia, US praise trilateral summit as 'success'
articles.title_zh: Leaders of China, Russia, US praise trilateral summit as 'success'
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

articles.title_orig: Social Security raise: What’s left after the Medicare premium hike?
articles.title_zh: Social Security raise: What’s left after the Medicare premium hike?
articles.content_orig:
Medicare's standard monthly Part B premium will rise by $6.50 in 2027, reducing the amount retirees keep from their Social Security checks.
Premiums will rise by 3.2 percent from $202.90 to $209.40 a month, while the annual Part B deductible will increase by $9 to $292, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) announced Tuesday.
The change comes as Social Security recipients await a 3.6 percent cost-of-living, or COLA, adjustment in the new year. The premium increase will absorb about 8.7 percent of the average $75 monthly retirement benefit boost, leaving about $68.60 a month before any other deductions.
The CMS increases, or more rarely decreases, the amount payable for Part B services every year. The department has said the rise this year owes mainly to "projected increases in healthcare spending."
Medicare Part B helps pay for doctors' services , outpatient hospital care, certain home health services, medical equipment and other services. The premium, paid monthly, is deducted from Social Security payments, reducing the overall amount deposited into a beneficiary's bank account.
The $75 figure is illustrative, based on average Social Security retirement payments, and how much an individual beneficiary will see their benefits boosted by is based solely on their own payments, though the Medicare cost increase is the same for all enrollees. Therefore, a person who gets a larger boost to their benefits due to the COLA will see a smaller drop in their benefits, while someone who only gets a more modest increase will see more of that absorbed by Medicare premiums.
Measured against the 3.6 percent COLA increase, the $6.50 premium hike would take about 12 percent of a $54 raise on a $1,500 benefit, leaving about $47.50, or 88 percent, of the increase. For a $3,000 monthly payment, it would take about 6 percent of the $108 raise, leaving about $101.50, or 94 percent, of the increase.
"In terms of cold, hard math, most will be marginally better off," David Kassir, managing director at Manna Wealth Management, told Newsweek . "That's because the 3.6 percent COLA is based on a percentage of one's benefit amount while the $6.50 increase in premiums applies equally (almost) to all. So those receiving more substantial Social Security checks will see dollar-for-dollar increases that more than make up for the higher Part B premium."
"But for those receiving less than average benefits, the COLA won't be as generous. And the Part B increase will have a greater impact," he continued. "Flat rate hikes hit hardest those receiving the smallest of Social Security checks. It's a nuance that's often lost in the shuffle."
The 2027 premium increase is the first time since 2023 that the Part B percentage increase is smaller than the COLA. Back then, the premium actually fell by 3.1 percent, while Social Security recipients received an outsized 8.7 percent boost to benefits, owing to heightened inflation as the U.S. came out of the coronavirus pandemic.
Alongside the Part B premium increase, other healthcare costs will rise for enrollees. The Part A hospital deductible, which covers inpatient hospital care, skilled nursing facilities, hospice, inpatient rehabilitation and some home health care, will rise by $40, from $1,736 in 2026 to $1,776 in 2027, while the daily coinsurance for longer hospital stays and skilled nursing facility care will also go up.
However, 99 percent of Medicare beneficiaries do not pay a Part A premium because they or their spouse have enough Medicare-covered work history, according to the CMS.
The COLA and new Medicare premiums will start in January 2027.

articles.title_orig: The view from the tower: Watch Starship come in for chopsticks catch in epic slo-mo video
articles.title_zh: The view from the tower: Watch Starship come in for chopsticks catch in epic slo-mo video
articles.content_orig:
The stunning return of Starship from the skies to a launch tower in South Texas answered some questions about the future of SpaceX’s ambitious rocket program. Namely, it is now rapidly moving toward rapidly reusable launch.
However, it raises other questions. For example, as Starship becomes fully reusable, when might humans fly on the vehicle?
The short answer is pretty simple: If SpaceX prioritizes human spaceflight on Starship, it could happen reasonably quickly. The longer answer becomes more complicated and depends on what one means by human spaceflight. The first people to fly on Starship probably won’t launch from Earth, or land here. Rather, they will probably be NASA’s lunar astronauts. So there are different timelines for humans flying aboard Starship and landing on Earth.
Given what is known publicly, and what Ars has heard privately, here are some educated guesses about all of this.
The first thing we can say for sure is that all estimates of human spaceflight on Starship should be taken with a gigantic grain of salt, including those in this article. Putting humans on any space vehicle is a difficult and time-consuming task, even outside of the requirements that NASA would impose for its astronauts.
The original target for launching humans on Starship (then known as the Interplanetary Transport System) set a decade ago was 2024. That was for a Mars mission. Then, in 2018 , SpaceX announced a lunar flyby mission on Starship with a target launch in 2023. This dearMoon mission was canceled in 2024. In 2022, SpaceX and Dennis Tito announced a lunar flyby mission later in the 2020s.
More recently, according to sources, SpaceX has been telling individuals interested in launching on Starship that it could begin offering flights by 2029. I probably would not put too much stock in this date.
All of this is to say, we cannot learn much from history other than to deeply discount any public launch dates on Starship for humans.
Most likely, the first humans to fly on Starship in space will do so after launching from Earth inside the NASA Orion spacecraft. Once in orbit they will then dock with Starship before transiting to the Moon, landing there in Starship, launching from the Moon back to Orion, and then returning to Earth inside NASA’s spacecraft.
NASA signed an agreement with SpaceX to develop Starship as this “Human Landing System” in 2021, with a lunar landing targeted for 2024. To no one’s surprise, this target has moved to 2028, and there remains considerable uncertainty about the viability of this date.
Nevertheless, the success of Saturday’s tower catch should help propel the Starship program toward a higher launch cadence, which is essential for lunar missions. It therefore seems plausible, but not certain, that humans could land on the Moon inside Starship before the end of this decade.
Again, how soon SpaceX achieves this target will depend upon its prioritization of a Human Landing System, among its other major goals to accomplish with Starship. At this point, SpaceX appears to be more focused on revenue-generating activities such as launching Starlink, and eventually, Starmind data center satellites.
Much has been made about the fact that Starship does not have a launch abort system—a feature of most human spacecraft that allows a crew vehicle to be rapidly pulled away from an exploding rocket.
This may not matter should SpaceX conduct its own human spaceflight missions. Unlike NASA, which imposes detailed human-rating requirements on vehicles carrying its astronauts, the Federal Aviation Administration does not certify commercial spacecraft as safe for passengers, instead operating under a regulatory framework that emphasizes informed consent and protection of the uninvolved public. Should SpaceX reach the point where it can launch Starship reliably, it will have the confidence it needs to press forward with human flights. Conceivably, this could happen within a few years.
According to potential customers, SpaceX is developing variants of the Human Landing System Starship for human flights, potentially carrying a few dozen people to the Moon. And such a prospect is tantalizing, for the interior of Starship’s pressurized cabin is almost unimaginably large for a spacecraft. A single Starship lunar lander has a pressurized habitable volume greater than the comparable volume of the International Space Station. This would be extraordinary.
Yet it is not a simple step to go from the current lunar lander design to an Earth lander. NASA’s lunar lander will never need to experience the tremendous heating of atmospheric reentry or perform the dramatic flip maneuver and propulsive landing that Starship uses to return home. Certifying those capabilities for human passengers, particularly on a vehicle without a traditional launch escape system, is an entirely different challenge.
Moreover, building a commercial human spaceflight business on Starship would be time-consuming and would likely not be nearly as profitable as launching Starlink satellites into space. And the risk is far greater—spaceflight remains dangerous, and the loss of a human crew would be a major negative for a publicly traded company. On the other hand, losing dozens of Starlink satellites on an errant launch would be a blip.
Despite Starship’s enormous theoretical capacity, SpaceX has also shown little interest in developing it as a crew transportation vehicle for commercial space stations in the near term. Several private space station operators have approached SpaceX about the possibility of Starship bringing astronauts to and from their stations. SpaceX indicated it was not interested.
Putting all of this together, I would not expect humans to land on Earth in Starship before 2030, and plausibly not until at least the mid-2030s.

articles.title_orig: Appeals court grants Trump request to halt order restoring Venezuelan TPS
articles.title_zh: Appeals court grants Trump request to halt order restoring Venezuelan TPS
articles.content_orig:
A United States appeals court has allowed the administration of President Donald Trump to move forward for now with the removal of deportation protections for Venezuelans .
The ruling on Wednesday cancels out a previous order by a lower-court judge that required the government to restore the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) of Venezuelans, which shields recipients against deportation.
The effort to end the TPS protections has proceeded despite humanitarian concerns .
Since taking office for a second term, Trump has sought to carry out what he calls the largest deportation effort in US history. Part of that agenda has been to roll back programmes like TPS.
But in September 2025, US District Judge Edward Chen blocked the expiration of TPS protections for Venezuelans, arguing that deporting those individuals would put them in harm’s way.
He also ruled that the Trump administration had overstepped its authority by seeking to shorten TPS extensions granted under the preceding president, Joe Biden. Such decisions, Chen added, needed to be taken with “careful study and analysis”.
Some 600,000 Venezuelans in the US were protected under TPS programmes.
The Supreme Court paused Chen’s ruling in October 2025. But that pause expired this month, and Chen’s order was set to take effect on Friday.
On Wednesday, the Trump administration filed an emergency request to the Supreme Court to extend the pause before Thursday’s appeals court ruling.
The appeals court’s decision does not nix the ongoing legal challenges to Trump’s efforts to revoke TPS extensions. But it allows the administration to suspend deportation protections while the challenges make their way through court.
The Trump administration has sought to strip large numbers of immigrants of their legal protections in a bid to render them deportable. Other programmes, like humanitarian parole, have also come under the administration’s scrutiny.
TPS allows foreign nationals already in the US to remain while conditions in their home countries are too dangerous or unstable to return to.
Humanitarian parole, meanwhile, allows people outside the US to come in on a temporary basis, often to escape similarly perilous conditions.
The Trump administration has argued that TPS designations are meant to be temporary — and that previous presidencies extended such protections without cause.
It has also maintained that conditions have improved in places like Venezuela, where a US military action on January 3 resulted in the abduction of President Nicolas Maduro.
Human rights advocates, however, have noted that Maduro’s government remains largely intact. That leadership has been accused of abuses ranging from arbitrary imprisonment to the torture of political dissidents.
The US Department of State currently warns against travel to Venezuela, citing issues such as crime, kidnapping and poor health infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: 6 things you should buy — and 5 things you definitely shouldn’t — during Black Friday and Cyber Monday 2026
articles.title_zh: 6 things you should buy — and 5 things you definitely shouldn’t — during Black Friday and Cyber Monday 2026
articles.content_orig:
NBC Selected independently determines what we cover and recommend. When you click on or buy through our links, we earn a commission. Learn more .
Retailers started rolling out their early Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals this week, so I’m sure you’ve asked yourself: are these discounts actually worth it? I’ve covered the massive sales for over six years, and I can say with certainty that they offer some of the year’s lowest prices across categories. But it takes a little bit of work to find the absolute best deals, and you have to strategize beforehand to save the most money.
To help you make a Black Friday and Cyber Monday game plan, I put together this guide filled with tips and tricks I swear by. I also talked to experts to get their advice about what to buy, what to skip, how to find the top deals and whether shopping in-person versus online makes a difference anymore.
Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter.
If you have electronics on your wish list — or are buying a gift for someone who does — now is your time to buy. Tech sees some of the strongest discounts during Black Friday and Cyber Monday, especially when it comes to devices like TVs , headphones and video game consoles , says Ashley Feinstein Gerstley , a shopping and savings strategist at Rakuten , an online and in-store cashback platform. As a baseline, Vipin Porwal , the founder and consumer savings expert at Smarty , an online shopping rewards app, expects at least 30 percent off in most cases, except for TVs and computers , which are usually in the 20 to 25 percent off range.
Black Friday and Cyber Monday video game bundles are particularly lucrative. It’s one of the only times a year I see brands like Nintendo , Xbox and PlayStation sell their most popular console, game and digital subscription for less than each item would cost if you bought them individually.
Toys is one of the most competitive categories during Black Friday and Cyber Monday, both in terms of discounts and demand. You usually get at least 30 percent off, says Porwal, and the most popular toys sell out quickly — I’m talking a couple of hours, maximum. Once you see prices drop, buy your must-haves immediately. Some of the hottest toys and collectibles to watch this season are the Beyblade X , Jellycats , KPop Demon Hunters toys , Lego Pokémon and SMART Play , NeeDohs , Pokémon Pikachu Puppetronic , Sesame Street Tickle Me Elmo Giggle Max and Toy Story 5 toys , according to Adobe .
Clothes and shoes typically get marked down by at least 20 to 25 percent during Black Friday and Cyber Monday, says Porwal. Many brands run sitewide sales, so their entire inventory is marked down, while department stores and big-box retailers put most of their stock on clearance to get rid of it before the new year.
Almost every small home and kitchen appliance you can think of gets discounted during Black Friday and Cyber Monday, including that Vitamix blender or Dyson vacuum you’re dreaming about. In addition to items you use year-round, keep an eye on seasonal appliances, like space heaters and snow blowers , as well as tableware , home decor and other essentials you’ll need to host guests during the holidays, says Gerstley.
Don’t forget to think beyond tangible products during Black Friday and Cyber Monday, says Mackenzie Shand, executive editor at RetailMeNot , a digital coupon, promo code and cashback platform. There are lots of deals on subscriptions, experiences and activities, too. “Many streaming services host Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales, which can lower the cost of your entertainment bill for the entire year,” she says. “Meanwhile, if you have travel plans coming up, be on the lookout for deals on things like passes to zoos, aquariums and other recreation-type places in your area.” Fitness classes, gym memberships, beauty appointments, educational platforms and event tickets also often drop in price.
Additionally, while Travel Tuesday, on December 1 this year, is a dedicated day for travel deals, you’ll start seeing offers well before then. Hotels, resorts, tour groups, rental home and car booking companies, cruise lines and flight booking platforms are starting to roll out their sales now, making it the ideal time to plan a trip. You’ll see travel essentials on sale, too, like suitcases , toiletry bags and packing cubes .
Because retailers know Black Friday and Cyber Monday are prime times for holiday shopping, many discount gift cards for literally everything: stores across categories, restaurants, movie theatres, spas, streaming services, food delivery platforms, and more. “As long as you plan to gift or use this gift card, you are basically getting free money from these deals,” says Shand. There are also strong discounts on gift sets, like those that bundle beauty products, gourmet food and beverages, travel essentials and accessories. You buy these sets, wrap them and give them to your recipient rather than having to curate a selection yourself.
No category is totally off limits during Black Friday and Cyber Monday — if you do the work, you can find a worthwhile deal on almost anything since the majority of retailers participate in the biggest shopping events of the year. But if you’re trying to narrow down your list, here’s what experts recommend waiting on and when to buy it instead:
No, Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals aren’t worse than last year, but they’re not dramatically better either, says Claudia Townsend , a consumer behavior researcher and expert and marketing professor at the University of Miami. “Prices have risen, while discount percentages are likely to remain roughly the same as last year,” she says. “This means that a 25 percent discount, for example, will yield a higher final price if the item’s starting price is higher than it was a year ago.”
That said, Black Friday and Cyber Monday are still the biggest, highest-revenue days for retail of the year. Retailers want to draw customers in with deals, so most save their lowest prices for late November. But a discount isn’t a compelling enough reason alone for shoppers to spend anymore, says Shand — they’re being much more thoughtful about scoping out real deals to get the best overall value, not just the lowest price.
“The most common mistake is allowing in-the-moment sales and marketing cues define one’s shopping list,” says Townsend. “That’s how people end up “saving” 40 percent on items they never intended to buy. I recommend that consumers create a list with a budget and a target price for each item, and commit to purchasing only when a deal reaches that price.”
Some retailers let you make shopping lists in their apps or on their websites and, along with certain cashback extensions, let you set up notifications when items’ prices drop so you can start evaluating immediately. That means you don’t have to do any browsing that might lead to impulse purchases — you stay zeroed in on your list the entire time.
Free tools like CamelCamelCamel , Keepa and Honey show you a product’s price history, as do built-in features on some retailers’ websites. Use them to determine whether an item dropped in price from a steady baseline, making it a legitimate deal, or if it’s marked down from an inflated baseline.
Be sure to also use price-tracking tools to figure out what a specific product cost during Black Friday and Cyber Monday last year. That serves as a great comparison point, especially for early deals: If a product’s price dropped more during last year’s Black Friday to Cyber Monday period than the two weeks before it, you can expect a brand to follow the same pattern this year, giving you an idea about when you should finally add to cart and check out.
Overall, “if the deal price matches or beats the item’s lowest price over the past year, it’s likely a good deal,” says Townsend.

articles.title_orig: USDA grapples with security breach as IT staff take multiple systems offline
articles.title_zh: USDA grapples with security breach as IT staff take multiple systems offline
articles.content_orig:
By David DiMolfetta and Jory Heckman
Numerous Department of Agriculture applications have been taken offline over a multi-day period in response to a cybersecurity incident internally disclosed earlier this week, according to three people familiar with the matter and an email viewed by Nextgov/FCW and Government Executive .
The outages have impacted many financial tools used to facilitate payments between the agency and farmers, said the people, who requested anonymity because details of the incident are sensitive. To help keep the nation’s food supply steady, USDA gives farmers a financial safety net for things like crop insurance or covering losses when factors like bad weather affect harvest yields.
It’s not clear who carried out the intrusion or if any data was exfiltrated from systems.
The department’s Cybersecurity and Privacy Operations Center “uncovered a security incident” that required its Information Services Division to “reset all database passwords in all environments, and this is requiring us to reset all applications causing outages,” per the email that was sent Monday by Chris Rottler, acting assistant chief information officer for USDA’s Farm Production and Conservation Business Center.
It’s unclear if all employees received this notice.
A technical bulletin dated Thursday that was also viewed by Nextgov/FCW and Government Executive says that maintenance activities are ongoing and that applications “may continue to experience intermittent outages throughout the week.” As of late Thursday afternoon, some staff were also experiencing issues with their virtual private network, or VPN, according to one of the people and a separate notice also viewed.
USDA and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency have been reached for comment.
Personnel across the department have grown frustrated over the last few days, the people say. The issues have prevented them from accessing key client-facing applications used to check important notifications and statuses of loans and other forms of aid, two of the people said.
High-level department officials also appear to have not been fully keeping USDA staff informed about the updates, the people added. One of the people said they had earlier been given vague information about a possible security breach, but that no other information had been provided.
Some staff initially unaware of the cyber incident have expressed concerns that the department could become the latest entity affected by widespread IT disruptions, following recent non-cybersecurity incidents that affected aviation networks , financial systems, Microsoft tools, and even the National Security Agency , two of the people said.
This story is breaking and may be updated.
Government Executive Staff Reporter Sean Michael Newhouse contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Cyberleek releases GTA 6 Xbox build, making playable PC port more realistic
articles.title_zh: Cyberleek releases GTA 6 Xbox build, making playable PC port more realistic
articles.content_orig:
Just when it seemed Cyberleek had disappeared for good, the notorious leaker has returned. Even though the GTA 6 release date has passed, the individual has followed through on past threats. A decrypted Xbox build is spreading through piracy networks, which could lead to a playable PC port . However, there is one major caveat with the 209 GB download.
The Cyberleek website now displays a message about the latest leak. While prior gameplay videos appeared to be from a PC-based development build , they elected to distribute GTA 6 Xbox files. Allegedly, this version is from November 2026, and images of a file structure exposing assets have emerged. Regardless, it may have limited use without the missing executable file.
Once again, Cyberleek hopes to raise cryptocurrency funds before releasing the critical file. Offering a playable build as the reward, they previously set a $30 million market capitalization goal for a meme coin. That October initiative failed, but hitting the $15 million mark will supposedly unlock the .exe.
Notably, a timer is also counting down from under 4 days. Once it expires, Rockstar ’s tormentor promises to circulate the executable on piracy sites anyway.
It's unclear how soon the GTA 6 Xbox files may result in a bootable game for PC users. Cyberleek believes hackers will find a way to emulate the console version for Windows within a week. As criticism of the 30 fps performance target continues, capable hardware could produce higher frame rates.
Unfortunately for pirates, no working Series X emulator currently exists. The hardware found in the Microsoft console and many PCs is similar, with CPUs sharing x86-64 architecture. Still, among other challenges, the Series X runs a custom OS that would need to be adapted for a Windows environment.
Another possibility is a decompilation project targeting the leaked GTA 6 Xbox files. Developers would analyze, modify, and reconstruct the code into a version that can boot on PCs.
Cyberleek also claims to possess a PS5 build as a fallback option. Besides accumulating cryptocurrency, the objective is to prevent console and PC ports from doubling Take-Two and Rockstar's profits.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic becomes most valuable AI firm in first-of-its kind IPO
articles.title_zh: Anthropic becomes most valuable AI firm in first-of-its kind IPO
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the public stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.
Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 per share , showing there is plenty of excitement around AI.
Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?
In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.5, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day, with shares hitting $97.
Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet (down 3%) and Amazon (down 3.9%).
The build-out happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.
The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.
"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."
While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.
The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate more quickly tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet.
It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.
As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.
The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.
That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.
Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.
With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.
"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.
So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth $1.5 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.
"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."
A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.
One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.
On Thursday, the same day Anthropic went public, a bipartisan group of lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.
A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.
Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.
Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".
"AI carries real risks," she added.
Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

articles.title_zh: Stocks plunge as investors take cover amid growing uncertainty
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Japan's SoftBank Group plunged 16.16% on Friday, leading a broader sell-off in Asian technology stocks following the highly anticipated market debut of artificial intelligence startup Anthropic .
SoftBank is one of the biggest backers of OpenAI, Anthropic's rival, having invested a total of $64.6 billion in the ChatGPT maker.
The sharp decline underscores growing investor concerns over SoftBank's aggressive bets on artificial intelligence, particularly its exposure to OpenAI, as markets question whether massive investments in AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns.
SoftBank's heavy exposure to OpenAI has made its shares particularly sensitive to shifts in sentiment toward the AI sector. The stock lost 30% in October and is down 31% so far this month.
If Friday's losses hold, it would be SoftBank's worst day in more than two years.
Japanese semiconductor stocks also tumbled, with Tokyo Electron falling 7.19%, Lasertec declining 6.75% and Renesas Electronics dropping 6.71%. That comes as AI darling Nvidia slid 2.9% overnight.
The sell-off extended to South Korea, where Nvidia suppliers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics dropped 6% and 4.7%, respectively. South Korea's benchmark Kospi also declined 3.66%.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell more than 2% overnight following Anthropic's highly anticipated Wall Street debut.

Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company ( TSM ) and equipment maker ASML ( ASML ) erased earlier gains Thursday, leading the Technology ( XLK ) sector lower.
Other areas of the AI trade also trimmed gains on Thursday, with optical equipment maker Coherent ( COHR ) trimming gains. Bloom Energy ( BE ) shares declined modestly. Neocloud providers CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and Nebius ( NBIS ) both erased gains to close down 6% and 9% respectively for the session.

articles.title_orig: Gap names new Athleta CEO, lowers full-year guidance
articles.title_zh: Gap names new Athleta CEO, lowers full-year guidance
articles.content_orig:
Gap Inc. on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec. 14.
Kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials. She was previously global brand president of Fabletics and began her career at Gap before that.
"I'm excited to return to Gap Inc. and partner with [Gap CEO Richard Dickson] and the team to strengthen our connection with customers and shape the brand's next chapter," Kechter said in a statement.
The announcement comes after Lululemon poached former Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be its chief product officer last month.
"Clearly, we're disappointed with Athleta's performance, and we recognize there's a lot of work ahead," Dickson told CNBC. "We had been in rebuild mode, but now we're really in turnaround mode."
Dickson said the company is focused on getting back to its fundamentals: fabrications, feature, form, function and fit. Dickson added that Kechter will be conducting a "comprehensive review" of the brand to reposition Athleta for future success.
While the execution of its strategy has thus far "fallen short," Dickson said this new approach will allow Athleta to fully realize its potential.
Gap also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings on Thursday and posted flat overall comparable sales. Wall Street had been expecting a comparable sales increase of 1.3%, according to StreetAccount.
Net sales grew 2%, though demand softened in October and early November due to warmer weather, the company said. Store sales increased 1%, while online sales increased 3%.
Gap also said it's recorded a $420 million adjustment to cost of goods sold and a $21 million adjustment to interest income from tariff refunds so far this year.
The company lowered its full-year net sales outlook to be "roughly flat," down from previous guidance of up between 1% and 1.5%. Gap is also now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $2.29 and $2.34, down from an earlier expectation of between $2.35 and $2.45 per share.
Dickson said in an interview that much of the lowered guidance was due to warmer weather in the first two weeks of the quarter, but he said Gap is expecting "meaningful acceleration" in shopping ahead of the peak holiday season.
"We're monitoring the trends, and we're going to remain agile as we respond to the changing business trends," Dickson said.
Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
For the quarter, Gap reported net income of $311 million, or 86 cents per share, compared with $236 million, or 62 cents per share, the year prior. Sales rose slightly from $3.94 billion the year prior.
At Athleta, net sales were down 14% compared with last year, coming in at $220 million. Comparable sales for the banner sank 15%, which the company attributed to "limited traction" from efforts to modernize its merchandise and marketing.
The company's namesake brand saw 9% comparable sales growth for the quarter, with net sales of $1.1 billion, marking an 11% increase compared with last year. Dickson said it was the brand's 12th consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales.
"Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency of the brand is really giving us confidence in the brand's ability to continue its momentum," Dickson said.
The Old Navy banner saw flat comparable sales for the quarter and net sales of $2.3 billion, up 1% compared with last year. It's the first earnings report since the brand, which has been experiencing sluggish sales, named Michael Francis as its new CEO last quarter. Francis began his role at Old Navy on Nov. 2.
Banana Republic saw its net sales sink 3% compared with last year, which the company attributed to delayed demand for cold-weather categories and a women's fall assortment that fell flat. Wall Street had been expecting growth of 1.5%, according to StreetAccount.
Dickson said the brand has since introduced new products and seen demand "rebound" as cooler weather has set in across the country.
"We've been encouraged by the early customer response, and we should see sequential improvement in the fourth quarter," he said. "There's some work to do here, but with peak selling still ahead, I'm confident that the team is focused on the right areas and [will] ultimately position Banana well for growth."

articles.title_orig: AMD Slides After Hunterbrook Shorts Stock, Cites Circular Deals
articles.title_zh: AMD Slides After Hunterbrook Shorts Stock, Cites Circular Deals
articles.content_orig:
Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."
Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.
The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."
The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.
"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."
Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.
AMD continued to slide after-hours, trading down 0.45% to $487 shortly after 4 p.m.
